newsitem.title: USA: House tax bill moving through panel little changed.
newsitem.headline: House tax bill moving through panel little changed.

text.p: A Republican-crafted tax bill was moving through the House tax-writing committee Thursday leaving components for families with children, education, and profits on investments largely intact.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, put together the bill for $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years to enact the tax portion of a budget agreement reached by congressional leaders and the White House last month.
In its second day of debate on the bill, the panel left provisions on a child tax credit, college education tax initiatives and capital gains tax reduction almost untouched.
To make a change in the bill, lawmakers were required to show their proposals would not push the net tax cut above the $85 billion ceiling.
Democrats made several attempts at trying to scale back the proposed capital gains tax cut to pay for changes they wanted in education tax relief and other areas. They were soundly defeated.

Republicans have put a high priority on reducing the tax on profits made from investments such as stocks. The Archer plan would cut the maximum capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from 28 percent for individuals and gradually reduce the rate for corporations to 30 percent from the current 35 percent.
Any bill approved by the House committee must pass the full House of Representatives; any differences with Senate legislation would need to be worked out before the tax bill could pass Congress.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, planned to unveil his tax legislation next week.
The House Ways and Means Committee turned back Democratic efforts to change education initiatives in the Republican tax bill to more closely mirror those proposed by President Clinton.

The committee's ranking Democrat, Rep. Charles Rangel of New York, offered a change that would have included Clinton's HOPE scholarship program to give a $1,500 tax credit for higher education in the bill. It was defeated.

Archer's bill would allow taxpayers to claim a HOPE tax credit for 50 percent of tuition up to $1,500. The administration has argued that would penalize students going to less-expensive schools like community colleges who would not then get the full tax credit.

The budget agreement called for "roughly" $35 billion in tax cuts over five years for Clinton's education tax initiatives. Archer's bill contains $31 billion for education tax initiatives, but the White House argued that only $22 billion of that amount went for the types of programs that were promised in the budget accord.
House Speaker Newt Gringich questioned Vice President Al Gore's assertion earlier this week that the Republican tax bill did not live up to the budget agreement.

"How would he know?" Gingrich said, adding that Gore was not in the room when the deal was made last month. "The deal he (Gore) described isn't the deal we made ..." The Georgia Republican said Gore "totally mischaracterized" the agreement.

The committee approved one Democratic amendment that would provide a tax credit of up to $150 for 50 percent of tuition costs for remedial tutoring programs for students in kindergarten through high school.
The committee defeated a measure to preserve the tax subsidies for ethanol, a corn-based fuel, worth billions of dollars a year to farmers.
The committee left the child tax credit provisions in Archer's plan untouched in Wednesday's session.

The child tax credit is the single biggest item in the proposed tax bill at a cost of $71 billion over five years. Under Archer's plan, families would receive a $400 tax credit in 1998 for each child under age 17, increased to $500 in the following years.
